title: Photography direction for a nonprofit
excerpt: Photograph the program as it actually happens, with consent, and reject distress as a hook. The pictures should argue that the work is real.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground, for a piece on choosing images that stay specific rather than theatrical.
caption: Color on a white ground, with the shape still readable. Pictures of a program should stay this clear. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should nonprofit photography show?
faqs.answer: A normal week of the program. The place, the task, and the people who agreed to be seen as agents. A visitor should be able to say what is happening. Abstract hands and a city from the air prove that a camera was hired, not that a service exists.

faqs.question: When should you not photograph participants?
faqs.answer: When they came for help, when they are minors under a stricter policy, or when being found would put them at risk. The default is privacy. Build a set that still works with staff who opted in, the materials, and the room. Need can be written without using someone's worst hour.

faqs.question: What is wrong with a sad hero image?
faqs.answer: It asks for a pulse instead of understanding. Participants can read it as being used. Thoughtful donors can read it as a lack of faith in the work. A true Tuesday, shot with permission, is harder to stage and easier to trust.

markdown:
Nonprofit website photography should show the work in the world. A donor or a participant deciding whether the work is real will read the pictures as claims. A sad photograph and a donate button, with no scene of the program, fails them. The frames are part of the argument. They show what a normal week looks like, who is acting, and what a visitor would be joining or funding.

Direct the pictures the way you direct a program description. What must be true in the frame, whose consent you have, what you will not stage. A founder or a program lead can make these calls before anyone picks up a camera. The camera is there to keep the record honest.

## The work, visible

The primary frame is the program doing its job. Boxes on a table at the school, with the hour implied by the light and the caption. A clinic desk set for intake, with no client's papers exposed. A crew on the segment they are responsible for, tools in use. A visitor should be able to say what is happening without reading a caption, and the caption should still add the day, the place, and the program name.

Show people as agents when they have agreed to be shown. Staff and volunteers doing the task. Participants when the relationship includes that permission and the image does not trade their dignity for a reaction. The default for anyone who came for help is privacy. Build a set that still works if every participant face is absent. If the set collapses without those faces, the set was leaning on them.

Include the place. Rooms, routes, counters, and buses are evidence that the program exists somewhere a person could go. Abstract color and clasped hands prove only that a photographer was hired. You can still care about light and framing. Care is not the same as vagueness. A specific room, shot with restraint, will do more for trust than a dramatic crop of an unnamed emotion.

If you run more than one program, do not let one photogenic scene stand for all of them unless the caption says so. A sports afternoon and a legal clinic are different worlds. Photograph the programs you want people to find. Reusing a single powerful frame on every page flattens the offer and, over time, starts to feel like a brand asset instead of a record.

## Consent before the shutter

Get permission in a form you can show a board. Who may be photographed, in what settings, for how long the image can stay up, and how someone withdraws. The conversation happens before the moment, not after a beautiful frame exists and the pressure to use it arrives. A withdrawal is honored by taking the image down, including from older posts you still control.

Minors, people in crisis, and anyone whose safety depends on not being found need a higher bar, often a bar of not photographing them at all. Photograph the staff who opted in, the materials, and the place. Tell the story of need in words that do not require a person's worst hour as illustration. If a funder asks for "more emotion," the answer is a clearer scene of the work, not a more exposed participant.

Staff consent matters too. A new hire did not agree to last year's shoot by joining the team. A person who has left should not remain the face of intake. Review the library when roles change. The about page and the homepage should show people a visitor might meet, or they should show the work without implying a personal introduction that will not happen.

Partners' spaces come with their own rules. A school, a clinic, a land manager. Get the shot list approved by the partner, not only by your communications volunteer. A frame that makes the partner look careless will cost you the room. Share selects before publication when the agreement says so. It usually should.

## What to reject

Reject the sad photograph used as a lever. Tears, empty cupboards staged for the camera, a person looking down while a logo hovers in the corner. These pictures may raise a pulse. They also tell a participant that your organization looks at them as an instrument. They tell a thoughtful donor that you do not trust the work to be interesting on its own.

Reject the gala as the definition of the organization. The room, the gowns, the giant check. One frame in a news note can record that a fundraiser happened. The homepage, the program page, and the proof should show the program. Donors who only see themselves at a party are being trained to fund the party.

Reject stock photography of generic distress, generic joy, or generic hands. Visitors can feel the stock, and participants can feel that the people in the pictures are not their people. A quiet, true, slightly ordinary frame from your own Tuesday is worth more than a polished file from a library. If you have no frames yet, publish none until you do, and let the sentences carry the page.

Reject frames that hide the work. A logo on a wall. A drone shot of a city. A handshake in a lobby. They fill a template. They do not answer "what do you do on a normal week?" That question is the whole assignment.

## Sequence, crop, and the phone

Plan the set as a sequence a page can use. One frame for the first screen, where the work is recognizable at a small size. One for the program page, with the practical scene. One for a proof, tied to the decision. Directing them as a set keeps the site from looking like a collage of unrelated moods.

Ask for a crop that survives a phone. The subject near the center, the critical action visible when the sides fall away. A wide banquet table with the relevant action at the far left will become a picture of a wall and a shoulder on a narrow screen. Shoot the vertical frame on purpose. Art direction includes the rectangle the site will actually display.

Do not put type across the only view of the work. Do not dim the scene under a dark veil so white letters will pop. The picture is evidence. Let it be as bright and as specific as the room was, and put the sentence beside it. Carousels that advance on their own will move the evidence while someone is reading it. If you show several frames, let the visitor move them, and make the first frame sufficient.

Captions carry the fact. Program, place, date. Alt text carries the scene for someone who cannot see it. "Volunteers sorting produce into family bags in a school gym" is alt text. "Impact" is not. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) places text alternatives under perceivable content. Non-text information needs a text form. Writing that sentence is part of the shoot, while the details are still remembered, not a chore for launch night.

## Weight, color, and honesty

These files are often the largest thing on the page. web.dev's [Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) name the failures a visitor feels. Largest Contentful Paint, when the main image finally appears. Cumulative Layout Shift, when the text jumps as the image arrives. Interaction to Next Paint, when a tap on Give or Apply waits. A huge uncompressed hero of a sad close-up fails the person twice. It loads slowly, and it was the wrong picture.

Export a phone crop and a wide crop. Reserve the space in the layout. Keep the color close to the room. A grade that turns every scene into amber tragedy is a form of the sad photograph, applied in software. Agree that the selects should look like the place on an ordinary day. Look at them on a normal phone, not only on the retoucher's display.

Keep permissions, selects, and alt text in one place the next editor can find. On a Hanabi project that place can be the client portal, with the brand files and the program sheets. The point is continuity. The person who launches the page should not be the only one who knows which frames are allowed to stay up.

## A shot list and a review

Write the list before the day. For each frame: the program, what must be visible, who has consented, what must stay out of frame, and which page it is for. "Homepage: pantry table at the east school, bags being packed, no student faces, vertical and horizontal." Hand that list to the photographer. Pretty surprises that violate the list are not selects.

Review against the list. Pass means the work is visible, the consent is in hand, and the frame is not asking for pity. A near miss that is more emotional than the pass is still a miss if it breaks the rule. Be willing to reshoot a setup or to publish with fewer images. Fewer is a legitimate outcome of direction.

Then remove the old stock and the old sad hero. Mixing one true Tuesday with three generic sorrows makes the true frame look accidental. The set should feel like one place, because you are one organization. Update captions when the program's day changes. A standing image of Wednesday pickup, after you moved to Thursday, is a small falsehood that participants will see first.

Look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) when you want the pictures and the page directed as one argument. Bring the program you most need to show, the consent rules you already believe, and any limits from partners. Leave with a shot list. A mood board is the wrong deliverable.

The frames will be judged on a phone, in a hurry, often by someone who needs the service. [The mobile visit for a nonprofit](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-nonprofit) is the next piece, because the first screen on a small device still has to show the work in the world and a way to give, join, or read the program.
